questions.text: We keep a written plan for each season: area, expected yield, and the inputs and labour we need.
We know our own average yield per acre for our main crops over the last 3 seasons.
We have a plan for a dry spell, flood or pest outbreak, such as early maturing seed, staggered planting or a second income.
Our income does not depend on one crop or one buyer for most of our sales.
We can get the seed, fertiliser and chemicals we need on time for planting, without delays.
We buy inputs from known suppliers such as agro-dealers or input credit providers, and can compare at least two.
We record who received which inputs, how much, and what they owe us.
Inputs we supply are checked for quality and expiry before use or resale.
We dry and clean our produce to a set moisture or quality standard before storing or selling.
Our store is clean, dry and pest-controlled, and we follow a written pest control routine.
We check quality at purchase or aggregation (moisture, foreign matter, damaged or germinated nuts) and reject or grade lots.
We know how much we lose after harvest and can name the main causes.
We use first-in first-out stock rotation and keep batch and stock records.
We have a written agreement (offtake, supply or purchase) with at least one buyer, covering volume, price basis and quality.
We know where each lot came from (member, village, date) and can show it to a buyer.
We know our buyers' quality and certification requirements and meet them.
We check current market prices from more than one source before we agree a price.
We delivered what our buyers ordered, on time, in the last 12 months.
Members elect leaders at a general meeting, and every member has one vote.
Members attend general meetings and receive a yearly report on money, sales and decisions.
Most members sell most of their crop through the group, and we know how much they sold outside it.
Members who use group inputs or credit repay on time, and we keep a record of who owes what.
Roles of leaders, managers and members are written down, and someone independent checks our books at least yearly.
Our savings group or cooperative savings is linked to the group's activities, with clear rules for loans.

questions.dimension: Seasonal cash flow and finance readiness
questions.text: We prepare a month-by-month cash plan across the season, showing when money comes in and goes out.

questions.dimension: Seasonal cash flow and finance readiness
questions.text: We keep a business bank or mobile money account separate from personal money.

questions.dimension: Seasonal cash flow and finance readiness
questions.text: We can show records of sales, costs and loan repayments for the past 2 to 3 seasons.

questions.dimension: Seasonal cash flow and finance readiness
questions.text: Repayment dates on any loan match when we get paid, such as after harvest.

questions.dimension: Seasonal cash flow and finance readiness
questions.text: We know how much money we need before harvest and where it will come from.
We know which regulators apply to us (FDA, TCDA, MOFA, Department of Cooperatives) and hold the registrations we need.
If we sell raw shea or cashew for export, we know about the TCDA permit and the development levy proof.
Our premises and products meet FDA requirements for what we do (storage, processing, labelling).
We are certified, or working towards certification, for the markets we want, for example organic, Fairtrade or the Global Shea Alliance programme.
Women in our group take part in decisions and have a say in how money from sales is used.
Women and young people can own or access the assets they need (land, trees, equipment) through our group.
Women and young people hold leadership roles or sit on committees.
We have a plan to look after our land, trees and water, for example tree planting, soil care and no bush burning.
